triage.name: Corns and Calluses
triage.reason: Common foot complaint with a clear diagnosis from history and focused skin exam; important in diabetes and footwear-related pressure.

demographics: Adults who stand or walk for long periods at work
More common in people who wear tight or poorly fitting shoes
Common in older adults as foot shape and fat pads change with age

risk_factors.text: Prolonged standing or walking (occupational or recreational)
Foot deformity such as bunions, hammertoes, or prominent metatarsal heads
Repetitive manual work or use of tools that rub the hands
Going barefoot or wearing thin-soled shoes on hard surfaces
Older age with thinning of the protective fat pads on the sole

social_history: Occupations requiring prolonged standing or walking
Frequent use of tight or high-heeled footwear
Sports or activities with repetitive friction on the hands or feet
exposures: Repeated friction or pressure from shoes, tools, or equipment

chief_complaints.text: I have a hard, thick patch of skin on my foot that hurts when I walk
There's a rough bump on my toe that rubs against my shoe
The skin on my hands has gotten thick and tough from my work

hpi.onset: Gradual over weeks to months of repeated pressure or friction
hpi.duration: Usually present for weeks to months before the patient seeks care
hpi.progression: Slowly thickens and enlarges with continued pressure; may become painful as it presses on deeper tissue
hpi.location: Corns on the tops or sides of toes and between toes; calluses on the soles, especially under the ball of the foot and heel; also on the palms and fingers
hpi.radiation: No radiation; discomfort stays at the site
hpi.quality: Hard, thickened, rough skin; pain is dull and pressure-like or sharp when pressed
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; often 2–5/10, worse with walking or standing
hpi.timing: Pain occurs mainly with weight-bearing or when shoes press on the area; may be constant if inflamed
aggravating: Walking or standing for long periods
relieving: Soaking the foot in warm water
Gently rubbing with a pumice stone

associated_symptoms.text: Thickened, hardened skin at the site
Pain or tenderness when pressure is applied
A small hard core in the center of a corn
Dry, scaly skin around the area
Redness or mild swelling if the area is irritated

pertinent_negatives: Numbness or tingling in the feet
Pain at rest or night pain
New or changing mole or growth

negatives: Joint stiffness lasting more than an hour in the morning
Numbness or tingling in the feet

atypical.how_it_differs: Neuropathy may blunt pain, so a corn or callus can go unnoticed until it ulcerates or becomes infected; any break in the skin needs urgent attention.
Thinning fat pads and foot deformities make calluses more likely and more painful; skin is thinner and more prone to breakdown.
Often related to sports, new shoes, or going barefoot; lesions are usually less thick and less painful than in adults.

general.mild: Well-appearing, ambulates without a limp, no distress
general.moderate: Well-appearing but favors the affected foot or hand when using it; mild discomfort with weight-bearing
general.severe: Well-appearing but limps or avoids weight-bearing on the affected area; visible discomfort when shoes press the lesion
general.critical: Not applicable; corns and calluses are not a critical illness

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin over pressure points (tops and sides of toes, between toes, soles, palms, fingers)
findings.finding: A well-circumscribed area of thickened, hardened, rough skin with preserved skin markings

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the sole under the ball of the foot or heel
findings.finding: A broad, flat, diffusely thickened plaque without a central core

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lesion on a toe and gently pare or probe the surface
findings.finding: A small, discrete, hard lesion with a central keratin core and a surrounding rim of thickened skin
Focal tenderness over the thickened skin

findings.maneuver: Squeeze the toe or forefoot from side to side
findings.finding: Pain reproduced by lateral compression of the affected toe or metatarsal area

findings.maneuver: Inspect the surface of the lesion for breaks in the skin
findings.finding: Skin is intact with no ulceration, fissure, or drainage

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the surrounding skin
findings.finding: No surrounding erythema, warmth, or induration

findings.maneuver: Test light touch and pinprick sensation in the feet, and check vibration or monofilament testing if neuropathy is suspected
findings.finding: Sensation is intact; no stocking-distribution sensory loss

findings.maneuver: Palpate the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses
Palpate the inguinal and epitrochlear lymph nodes
findings.finding: No enlarged or tender lymph nodes

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the joints of the foot and hand
findings.finding: No joint swelling, effusion, or deformity beyond the pressure-related lesion

findings.text: No bony abnormality; thickened soft tissue over the pressure point
Underlying bony prominence, such as a prominent metatarsal head, bunion, or hammertoe, that explains the pressure point
No fracture, dislocation, or bone destruction
Focal thickening of the epidermis and dermis over the pressure point with no soft tissue mass
No bone marrow edema, abscess, or soft tissue mass
Thickened hyperechoic epidermis over the lesion with no discrete mass or fluid collection

initial.why: Confirms the diagnosis by showing a well-circumscribed area of hyperkeratosis with preserved skin markings and no ulceration, drainage, or surrounding cellulitis
Identifies the pressure or friction source that must be removed for the lesion to resolve
Looks for an underlying bony prominence or deformity that explains the pressure point
initial.only_if: the lesion is atypical, recurrent, or a bony deformity is suspected

supporting.why: Distinguishes a corn or callus from a soft tissue mass, abscess, or bone infection
supporting.only_if: a deep mass, abscess, or osteomyelitis is suspected

supporting.why: Can confirm a thickened epidermis and exclude a fluid collection or mass when the diagnosis is uncertain
supporting.only_if: the diagnosis is uncertain or a fluid collection is suspected

not_indicated.why: No role in an uninfected pressure lesion; a normal white count does not change management
Not needed unless infection or osteomyelitis is suspected
Not needed unless infection or osteomyelitis is suspected
Routine chemistry is not relevant to a mechanical skin lesion
Not part of the workup for the lesion itself; screen for diabetes only if there is a separate clinical reason
Not routine for a typical corn or callus; reserve for atypical, recurrent, or deformity-associated lesions
Not routine; reserve for suspected mass, abscess, or osteomyelitis
Not routine; reserve for diagnostic uncertainty

decision_points: Check for diabetes and peripheral arterial disease before any debridement or self-treatment, because these patients are at high risk of ulceration and infection
Look for an underlying bony deformity or biomechanical problem when the lesion recurs despite proper footwear
Refer to podiatry or orthopedics when the lesion is painful, recurrent, or associated with a deformity that needs correction
Do not shave or cut off a corn or callus at home; this can cause infection

differential.name: Plantar wart
differential.why_considered: A painful, thickened lesion on the sole or toe that can look like a callus or corn

history: Onset may be more rapid than a callus
May have appeared without a clear change in footwear or activity
Often painful with direct pressure, sometimes with squeezing
exam: Loss of normal skin markings over the lesion
Thrombosed capillaries (small black dots) visible after gentle paring
Pain with lateral (side-to-side) squeezing of the lesion
Discrete, well-demarcated lesion rather than a broad diffuse plaque

differential.name: Diabetic foot ulcer
differential.why_considered: A foot lesion in a patient with diabetes or neuropathy, where a callus can break down into an ulcer
differential.trigger: Any break in the skin, drainage, or a non-healing foot lesion in a patient with diabetes or peripheral neuropathy

history: Diabetes mellitus, often with peripheral neuropathy
May be painless because of sensory loss
Non-healing or worsening despite offloading
exam: Open wound, ulceration, or fissure with a break in the skin
Surrounding callus with a punched-out ulcer beneath it
Reduced sensation on monofilament or vibration testing
Possible drainage, foul odor, or surrounding cellulitis
labs: Elevated white blood cell count, CRP, or ESR if infected
imaging: Foot x-ray showing soft tissue defect, gas, or bone changes if osteomyelitis is present
MRI showing marrow edema or abscess if deep infection is suspected

differential.name: Verruca vulgaris (common wart)
differential.why_considered: A rough, thickened skin growth on the hands or feet that can resemble a callus

history: May appear without repetitive friction or pressure
Often asymptomatic or mildly tender
May spread to other sites
exam: Loss of skin markings
Thrombosed capillaries (black dots) after paring
Discrete, exophytic, or cauliflower-like surface
Pain with lateral compression rather than direct pressure

differential.name: Foreign body granuloma
differential.why_considered: A focal, tender, thickened area on the sole or hand after a puncture or embedded material

history: History of a puncture wound or stepping on something
Persistent focal pain or a feeling of something in the skin
May have had a minor injury weeks earlier
exam: Focal induration or a visible or palpable foreign body
Surrounding hyperkeratosis may be present but is not the primary lesion
Tenderness localized to a small point
imaging: Foot x-ray or ultrasound may show a radiopaque or echogenic foreign body

differential.name: Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin
differential.why_considered: A persistent, thickened, or non-healing skin lesion on the foot or hand that can be mistaken for a callus
differential.trigger: A lesion that is growing, bleeding, ulcerated, or not healing despite removal of pressure

history: Lesion is growing or changing over weeks to months
May bleed or crust
Not explained by friction or pressure
May have a history of sun exposure or prior skin cancer
exam: Indurated, firm, or friable lesion
Ulceration, crusting, or bleeding
Irregular borders or a raised rolled edge
May be fixed to underlying tissue
imaging: Biopsy is required for diagnosis; imaging is not diagnostic

differential.name: Tinea pedis (with hyperkeratotic changes)
differential.why_considered: Thickened, scaly skin on the sole that can resemble a callus

history: Itching is common
May have a history of athlete's foot or nail fungus
Often bilateral and diffuse rather than focal
exam: Scaling, fissuring, or maceration, especially between the toes
Diffuse involvement of the sole rather than a focal pressure point
Possible nail changes (thickening, discoloration)
labs: KOH preparation or fungal culture positive for dermatophytes

differential.name: Psoriasis (palmoplantar)
differential.why_considered: Thickened, scaly plaques on the palms or soles that can look like calluses

history: History of psoriasis elsewhere on the body
May be bilateral and symmetric
Often not limited to pressure points
exam: Well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale
Involvement of palms and soles in a symmetric pattern
Nail pitting or onycholysis
Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding when scale is removed)

differential.name: Osteomyelitis
differential.why_considered: Deep foot pain and swelling in a patient with a foot lesion, especially with diabetes
differential.trigger: Fever, deep pain, or a non-healing ulcer over a bony prominence in a patient with diabetes or vascular disease

history: Fever, chills, or malaise
Deep, constant pain that may be worse at night
Non-healing ulcer or recent foot infection
exam: Fever
Focal bone tenderness
Overlying ulcer or sinus tract
Surrounding cellulitis
labs: Elevated white blood cell count, CRP, and ESR
imaging: Foot x-ray showing bone destruction, periosteal reaction, or lucency
MRI showing bone marrow edema and enhancement

severity.mild: Small, painless or minimally tender area of thickened skin that does not limit activity
severity.moderate: Thicker, painful lesion that causes discomfort with walking or manual work but no skin breakdown
severity.severe: Large or multiple painful lesions that limit weight-bearing or hand use, or are associated with significant disability
severity.critical: Not applicable; corns and calluses are not life-threatening

red_flags.meaning: Suggests ulceration or infection; urgent evaluation and treatment are needed, especially in diabetes
Suggests cellulitis or deeper infection; requires prompt medical evaluation

red_flags.finding: Loss of sensation in the feet
red_flags.meaning: Suggests peripheral neuropathy; the patient may not feel the lesion and is at high risk for ulceration
Suggests peripheral arterial disease; poor healing and higher risk of infection

red_flags.finding: Rapidly growing, bleeding, or non-healing lesion
red_flags.meaning: Raises concern for malignancy or infection; biopsy or further workup may be needed

complications.name: Ulceration
clues: Break in the skin over the lesion

complications.name: Osteomyelitis
clues: Non-healing ulcer over a bony prominence

special_populations.differences: Neuropathy may mask pain, so lesions can go unnoticed until they ulcerate or become infected; any break in the skin needs urgent attention and offloading.
Thinning fat pads and foot deformities make calluses more likely and more painful; skin is thinner and more prone to breakdown.
Often related to sports, new shoes, or going barefoot; lesions are usually less thick and less painful than in adults.

key_questions.question: Where exactly is the thickened skin, and how long has it been there?
key_questions.looking_for: A focal area over a pressure point (tops or sides of toes, between toes, ball of the foot, heel, palms or fingers) present for weeks to months

key_questions.question: What kind of shoes do you wear, and have you changed footwear recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Tight, narrow, high-heeled, or poorly fitting shoes; new shoes or boots; identifies the friction source

key_questions.question: Do you stand or walk for long periods at work or during activities?
key_questions.looking_for: Occupational or recreational prolonged standing, walking, running, or repetitive manual work

key_questions.question: Does it hurt when you press directly on it, or when you squeeze it from the sides?
key_questions.looking_for: Pain with direct pressure favors a corn or callus; pain with side-to-side squeezing favors a plantar wart

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any break in the skin, drainage, or an open sore?
key_questions.looking_for: Any ulceration, fissure, or drainage, which suggests breakdown or infection rather than a simple pressure lesion

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, poor circulation, or numbness or tingling in your feet?
key_questions.looking_for: Diabetes, peripheral arterial disease, or peripheral neuropathy, which raise the risk of ulceration and infection

key_questions.question: Have you tried to cut, shave, or use medicated pads or acids on it?
key_questions.looking_for: Self-treatment that may have caused injury or infection; medicated corn plasters can damage skin

key_questions.question: Is the area red, warm, swollen, or spreading?
key_questions.looking_for: Signs of cellulitis or deeper infection

key_questions.question: Have you had a puncture wound, stepped on something, or had a foreign body in the foot or hand?
key_questions.looking_for: A retained foreign body or granuloma that can mimic a focal callus

key_questions.question: Do you have any other skin conditions, such as psoriasis or athlete's foot?
key_questions.looking_for: Palmoplantar psoriasis or tinea pedis that can cause thickened, scaly skin

key_questions.question: Any fever, chills, or feeling unwell?
key_questions.looking_for: Systemic symptoms suggesting infection; usually absent in uncomplicated corns and calluses

key_questions.question: Is the lesion growing, bleeding, or failing to heal despite removing pressure?
key_questions.looking_for: Features concerning for malignancy or a non-healing ulcer, which require biopsy or urgent evaluation

accepted_names: Hyperkeratosis due to pressure or friction
reasoning_points: A focal area of thickened, hardened skin at a site of repeated pressure or friction
Location over a pressure point: tops or sides of toes and between toes for corns, soles and palms for calluses
Gradual onset over weeks to months, worse with walking, standing, or manual work
Preserved skin markings and no black dots, favoring a corn or callus over a wart
Skin is intact with no ulceration, drainage, or surrounding cellulitis
Sensation and pedal pulses are intact, making neuropathy and peripheral arterial disease less likely
Symptoms improve with removal of pressure, better-fitting shoes, and non-medicated padding
Diabetes, neuropathy, or poor circulation are checked for because they change management and raise the risk of ulceration

easy: Adult with a hard, thickened patch on the sole or a toe that hurts when walking
Clear history of tight or poorly fitting shoes or prolonged standing
Well-circumscribed hyperkeratosis with preserved skin markings and no ulceration
Symptoms improve with offloading and better footwear
medium: Lesion between the toes that is hard to see and mimics tinea pedis
Painful lesion on the ball of the foot with an underlying bony prominence or hammertoe
Patient with diabetes and a callus that needs careful skin and sensation checks
Lesion on the hands from repetitive manual work rather than the feet
hard: Callus over a bony prominence in a patient with neuropathy that is painless and could hide an ulcer
Lesion that does not heal after pressure is removed, raising concern for malignancy or infection
Plantar wart mistaken for a callus because of similar location and thickening
Older adult with thin fat pads, foot deformity, and multiple painful calluses
Chronic plaque on the sole that is actually palmoplantar psoriasis
